Instant
IN-stant
adjective
From the Latin instans, present participle of instare, “to stand upon, to press upon, to urge” (in, “upon,” + stare, “to stand”); hence urgent, pressing. The modern noun for a moment came from the sense of a pressing, present point of time.

Biblical Definition

Instant in the KJV is never the modern noun for a fleeting moment; it is an adjective and adverb meaning urgent, pressing, insistent — to be instant is to press a matter hard and not let go. Paul bids the Romans be “continuing instant in prayer” (Rom 12:12), not praying briefly but praying with an unrelenting importunity that keeps its hold on God. He charges Timothy, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — stand to it, urge it, press it whether the hour seems fit or not, with all longsuffering and doctrine. The word describes the earnestness of men in dead earnest. The elders of the Jews “besought him instantly” for the centurion (Luk 7:4), pressing the Lord with reasons; and in a darker use the same insistence turns murderous, for the crowd before Pilate “were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified” (Luk 23:23), and their instancy prevailed. So the word cuts both ways: the same pressing urgency that storms heaven in prayer can storm a judgment-hall for blood. What Scripture commends is holy instancy — the widow who wearied the unjust judge, the friend at midnight who would not be denied, the wrestling Jacob who said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me. The Christian’s prayer is not a polite request lightly withdrawn; it is an instant, importunate, God-honouring refusal to release the promise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Urgent; pressing; earnest and importunate — not a fleeting moment.

INSTANT, urgent; pressing; earnest; importunate.

From Latin instare, “to stand upon, to press upon.”

The modern noun for a moment came of a pressing point of time.

Continuing instant in prayer (Rom 12:12); instant in season (2Ti 4:2).

The crowd was instant with loud voices for the crucifixion (Luk 23:23).

Key Scripture

Rom 12:12 — "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;"

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Luk 7:4 — "And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this:"

Luk 23:23 — "And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed."

Modern Corruption

An honest drift from “urgent” to “a moment”; the word recovers the importunate, pressing earnestness Scripture commends in prayer and preaching.

expand to see more

The modern reader knows “instant” only as a name for the briefest span of time, or as a promise of coffee made without waiting; and so he cannot hear what Paul means by “continuing instant in prayer.” The AV’s instant is not a moment but an urgency — a pressing, insistent, importunate holding-on. To read the modern sense into Rom 12:12 is to make the verse counsel brief prayer, when the apostle counsels unrelenting prayer — the very opposite of a passing instant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is holy importunity. Our Lord taught it in the widow who wearied the unjust judge and the friend who knocked at midnight and would not go away; He commended the woman of Canaan whose faith would not be refused. To be instant is to press the promise and not let go, to preach in season and out of season, to plead until the blessing come. The world’s instancy can turn murderous, as the crowd was instant for the crucifixion; but sanctified, it is the wrestling of Jacob, who said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me. God is not wearied by such prayer; He is honoured by it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means urgent, pressing, importunate — not a fleeting moment.

expand to see more

Instant — Latin instare, “to press upon, to urge.”

It means urgent, insistent, earnest in the pursuit.

The modern noun for a moment is a later branch of the word.

Continuing instant in prayer (Rom 12:12).

Be instant in season, out of season (2Ti 4:2).

Usage

"“Continuing instant in prayer” is unrelenting prayer, not a brief one."

"To be instant is to press the matter hard, in season and out of season."

"The crowd was instant for the crucifixion: even instancy can turn murderous."
